Engineering/The hidden problem

Engineering · Tracking in Africa

The hidden problem behind logistics, delivery and ride-hailing in Africa, and how we solved it.

This project was possible because of Claude, which sped up the testing, the iteration and the design.

01 The problem

Every logistics, delivery and ride-hailing app runs on one core feature: tracking.

Ask anyone in Africa who uses these apps. Many of them are clunky, and they always seem a step behind. That's a big part of why they don't feel as smooth as Uber, Bolt or Lyft.

Here's a simple example. Say you live in Sea Point, Cape Town, South Africa, and you order from a restaurant in Gardens, about 5 km away.

If you order in the app, finding you is easy. The rider follows the pin you dropped.

Now say you phone the order in instead. The person who answers might be a support agent, a dispatcher, or someone at an ambulance call centre, and they can't see where you are. So they have to:

They need to do all of this before the call ends, so you know what you're paying for. It's slow, and it happens on every single call.

I don't know exactly how every company tracks its vehicles. But I've worked at a few startups and seen how people run these systems. Most setups are slow, unreliable and clunky:

  • Positions show up late.
  • Distances on the map jump around.
  • "Nearest rider" usually means nearest in a straight line, not by road.

This matters more now than it did a few years ago. As apps like Uber pull out of some markets, new ride-hailing apps keep launching to fill the gap. But they can't match the maps and tracking the big players have.

Those companies spent millions on this one problem. They hired some of the best engineers in the world and gave them years to solve it. A small team can't spend that kind of money, and it can't spend that long on one problem.

So most teams end up with one of two bad choices:

Bad choice 1

Pay for a maps API.

Every distance lookup costs money. The bill grows with every order and every rider, and it grows fastest when business is good.

Bad choice 2

Use straight-line distance.

It's free, but often wrong. A rider 800 m away across a river can be 15 minutes away by road.

So I decided to take a jab at this problem. In this article, I walk you through how I did it.

02 What we built

The breakthrough came from the infrastructure.

It isn't a clever new algorithm. It's proven tools, fitted together.

If I had written every part in my own code, I'd have spent months on problems other people had already spent years and a lot of money solving.

So I picked proven tools instead. Each one has been tuned for years by people who think about that one job all day. Then I fitted them together.

Picture one block in the middle: the tracking system. Around it sit six tools. Each one is great at one job, and each one plugs into the middle.

Building this took more DevOps knowledge than coding: knowing how each tool runs, how they talk to each other, and how to keep them alive on a server. The rule was simple: don't rebuild what a proven tool already does well.

Here's what the system does, and why each piece matters to you.

How positions get from the phone to the system

Phones send their positions over MQTT, a messaging protocol built for small devices on weak networks.

Most apps send each position as a normal web request. The phone opens a connection, sends headers, waits for a reply, then does it all again 5 seconds later. MQTT opens one connection and keeps it open, so each position is a tiny message sent down a pipe that's already there.

For the rider, that means less battery drain. For you, it means positions keep arriving even on patchy 3G at the edge of town.

Every phone has its own login, and it can only send its own position.

One rider's phone can't pretend to be another rider. If a phone gets cloned or stolen, you lose that one phone, not your whole fleet.

The login is checked once, when the phone connects, not on every ping.

A rider starts a shift. The phone connects and logs in, and that's one database check. Over the next few hours, the phone sends a thousand positions.

The first one needed a check. The other 999 didn't, because the connection was already trusted.

A system that checks every ping would hit its database thousands of times a second, just to ask "is this phone still allowed?" This approach asks once per connection. The database stays small, cheap and fast, and it's free for the questions that really need it.

Each ping is light, because it doesn't carry a login token.

Some setups attach a signed token (a JWT, often several hundred bytes) to every single position. This approach doesn't need to, because the connection is already trusted.

Here's what that saves:

  • A rider pings every 5 seconds over a 10-hour shift. That's about 7,200 pings a day.
  • At about 500 extra bytes each, that's about 3.6 MB a day per rider.
  • Over a month of shifts, that's about 100 MB per rider.
  • Across 100 riders, that's roughly 10 GB a month.

The chart below adds this up over a year. The grey bar is the data that does real work: the position itself. The orange bar is the extra data a JWT on every ping would send. Our approach sends no token, so it never sends the orange bar at all. Move the riders slider to see it for your own fleet.

If your company pays for riders' data bundles, those 10 GB are money you spend every month on bytes that do nothing.

If your riders pay for their own data, it's worse. Each rider loses about 100 MB of their own bundle every month, just to send tokens nobody needed. For someone earning per delivery, that's a real pinch, and it comes out of their pocket, not yours.

Finding the right rider

When your system asks "where is this rider?", the answer comes back in milliseconds.

There's no database query in the way. So the answer stays fresh and fast even when thousands of phones are pinging the servers at once.

When your system asks "who's nearest to this pickup?", it only looks at the area around the pickup, not at every vehicle in the city.

That's why it stays just as fast whether you run 100 riders or 10,000 drivers.

The ranking looks at which way each driver is heading.

Picture a courier company with a depot in Paarden Eiland. A parcel is ready to go, and two vans are nearby:

  • Van A is 300 m away and driving back toward the depot.
  • Van B is 200 m away, but it has just left the depot and is heading out onto the N1, the other way.

On a straight-line ranking, Van B wins because it's closer. But Van B would have to find an exit, turn around and come back. Van A is already on its way in. A good dispatcher picks Van A, and so does the system.

It can rank drivers by real road distance, and it does this on your own servers.

There's no per-request bill, and the driver across the river drops down the list, where they belong.

Knowing when a vehicle arrives or leaves

You draw an area on the map, and the system tells you the moment a vehicle enters or leaves it.

The area can be a circle or any shape. You don't need a script that checks positions every few seconds.

Each alert fires exactly once, and here's why that matters:

  • If an alert sends a one-time code to a customer, they should get one code, not three.
  • If it texts a car owner, three texts in a row feel like spam, or like panic.
  • If each message is an SMS you pay for, you'd pay three times for one event.

How your system hears about it

When something happens, the tracking system calls your server with a signed message, called a webhook.

The signature lets your server check that the message really came from the tracking system. Some hacky script pretending to be the system can't fake it.

If your server is down, the tracking system keeps retrying for up to 10 hours.

Say your server crashes at 1 a.m. At 1:15 a.m., one of your customers' cars leaves its parking zone. It's being stolen.

Without retries, that alert is gone. By the time anyone notices, the car is 100 km away and already stripped for parts.

With retries, the alert keeps knocking. If your server is back within the hour, you get that alert as soon as it's up, while there's still a chance to act.

Every customer gets its own delivery lane.

One customer's slow server can never hold up another customer's alerts.

Replaying where a vehicle has been

Every position is stored, because most arguments in this business are about where someone was.

Did the rider really wait at the gate? Did the truck actually drive down that street? Did the van stop for two hours with the doors open?

Without history, those questions turn into one person's word against another's. With history, you replay the trip and look.

You can view any trip three ways: the raw points, a smoothed line, or the path snapped onto real roads.

One customer's data can be erased with a single command.

You'll need that when a customer leaves you, or asks for their data to be deleted under privacy law.

Cutting off a phone in about a second

Not every phone in your fleet will behave. Some are lost, some are stolen, and some are being used to cheat.

Plus, people are finding new ways to beat these systems all the time:

  • Fake locations. A rider installs a GPS spoofing app so their phone claims to sit right outside the busiest restaurant in town. The system keeps offering them the best orders, even though they're at home on the couch 6 km away. Honest riders lose those orders.
  • Spam. Someone pulls the login out of the rider app and writes a script that floods your servers with thousands of fake positions a minute.
  • Theft. A phone gets snatched halfway through a delivery, and whoever has it now has an app that can send positions into your fleet.
  • Mix-ups. A rider leaves their phone at home and starts the shift on a second phone, or stays logged in on two devices at once.

Whatever the reason, you revoke that one phone. Within about a second, its connection is cut. Every time it tries to reconnect, it's refused.

Here's what that looks like. Your system sends one request:

Request
POST /v1/devices/7f3c2a91-4b6e-4d2a-9c1e-2b8f5d0a6e13/revoke
X-API-Key: <your API key>
Response · the device, now turned off
{
  "id": "7f3c2a91-4b6e-4d2a-9c1e-2b8f5d0a6e13",
  "external_id": "CA 123-456",
  "label": "Sipho's motorbike",
  "username": "capeeats.CA 123-456.k4p9",
  "status": "revoked",
  "mode": "motorcycle"
}

The rest of your fleet doesn't notice a thing. And if you ever need to stop a whole customer account, all of its phones drop within seconds.

Room to grow

  • It handles 100 vehicles just as easily as 10,000. You don't rebuild anything as you grow. You add servers.
  • It runs on three small servers. If one dies, the other two carry on, and no positions are lost.

What this frees your team to build

Tracking is like plumbing. Every company in this space needs it, and most build it badly.

That's not because their engineers are bad. It's because tracking isn't their product. They have deadlines and limited cash, and they can rarely afford engineers who specialise in maps and real-time data.

When the plumbing just works, developers get their weeks back. They can spend them on things customers actually see, like:

That's the quick tour. Now let's open it up, starting with the one rule the whole system rests on.

03 The big picture

Every position goes into one log first.

Here is the whole system on one page, then the tools, and why each one beat the obvious choice.

The tools I picked, and why each one beat the obvious choice

Why NATS instead of an MQTT broker plus Kafka

Most developers build this part from three separate pieces:

  1. an MQTT broker (like Mosquitto or EMQX) to receive positions from phones,
  2. Kafka next to it, to keep a log of positions you can replay,
  3. a separate login service to decide which phones may connect.

It works, but it's clunky, and here's why it hurts:

  • There are three systems to install, upgrade, watch and pay for. Each has its own settings, its own logs and its own ways of failing.
  • Something has to copy messages from the broker into Kafka. That bridge is yet another program. When it breaks, positions pile up or quietly go missing.
  • When something fails, there are three places to check. At 2 a.m., three suspects is two too many.
  • Kafka is heavy. It was built for huge companies. It's a lot of machine and a lot of know-how for a fleet of a few thousand vehicles.

NATS does all three jobs in one small program. It speaks MQTT to the phones, keeps the replayable log itself (a feature called JetStream), and asks the login service about every new connection (NATS calls this the "auth callout").

That's one program, one set of logs and one place to look. NATS is also very fast and light, because it was built for exactly this kind of traffic: lots of small messages, all the time.

Why live positions sit in memory instead of in Redis

The latest position of every vehicle lives in plain memory, inside each API server.

The obvious choice would be Redis, a popular database that also keeps data in memory. The catch is that Redis runs as its own server, so every search has to cross the network to Redis and back.

  • Reading from local memory takes well under a millisecond.
  • A round trip across the network costs about a millisecond or more, every time, before any real work is done.

The whole point of keeping data in memory is speed, and that network trip would eat most of it.

Redis would also be a second copy of the truth that has to be kept in sync. Instead, each API server rebuilds its own copy from the message log when it starts. There's one source of truth, and nothing to keep in sync.

Why H3 hexagons instead of PostGIS

PostGIS is the standard tool for maps inside a database, and it's excellent. But for live "who's nearby?" searches, it has two problems.

Every search becomes a database query. The request goes over the network, the database plans and runs the query, and the answer comes back. That takes milliseconds.

The database has to keep up with every single ping. To give correct answers, it needs the latest position of every vehicle. So it takes thousands of writes a second, all day long, just to stay current.

H3 is Uber's open-source hexagon grid. It cuts the map into hexagon-shaped cells. Working out which cell a point is in, and which cells surround it, is pure maths done in memory. It takes about a microsecond, which is a thousandth of a millisecond.

At 10,000 vehicles, that gap decides whether a search feels instant or starts to crawl.

Why Tile38 instead of writing geofence code from scratch

To build alerts from scratch, I'd need to:

  • run a loop that checks every vehicle against every zone, over and over,
  • write my own "is this point inside this shape?" maths,
  • catch the exact moment a vehicle crosses an edge, not just whether it's inside right now.

That last one is harder than it sounds, because GPS jitters. A phone's reported position wobbles by several metres, even when it isn't moving.

Picture a car parked right on the edge of a zone. Its dot wobbles across the line: in, out, in, out, every few seconds. Simple code fires "entered!", "left!", "entered!", "left!", and the customer gets a flood of alerts about a car that never moved.

There's an opposite problem too. Picture a thin zone, like a 50 m area at a gate, and a fast car that pings every 5 seconds. One ping lands just before the zone, and the next lands just after it. The car drove straight through, but no ping ever landed inside. A simple "is it inside?" check misses it completely.

Tile38 is a database built for exactly this, with years of tuning behind it. It compares each new position with the last one, works out real crossings, and pushes a message the moment one happens. On top of that, each alert fires only once, so even a jittery edge can't spam anyone.

Why ClickHouse stores the history instead of Elasticsearch, Postgres or Timescale

History is billions of tiny rows, each one saying "this vehicle was here at this time." And almost every question is the same: show me this vehicle between these two times.

Here's how the usual options cope:

  • Elasticsearch is built for searching text, like finding every log line that mentions an error. It stores a lot of extra index data to make that fast. For billions of positions, you pay in disk and memory for search features you'll never use, and it's a heavy system to run.
  • Postgres stores data row by row, and every row carries about 20 to 30 bytes of bookkeeping. A position is only a few numbers, so the bookkeeping can be as big as the data itself. With billions of rows, the indexes balloon and the database gets slower as it grows.
  • Timescale is Postgres with time-series features added, and its compression helps a lot. But it's still Postgres underneath, so it's still heavy to run at this size.

ClickHouse stores data by column instead of by row. All the latitudes sit together, and so do all the longitudes. Similar numbers stored side by side compress extremely well, so each stored position takes about 26 bytes.

ClickHouse also keeps each vehicle's rows together on disk, in time order. So "show me this rider's day" reads one small, tight block. And deleting one customer's data is cheap.

Why Valhalla instead of paying for a maps API

Valhalla is an open-source routing engine. It works out real driving routes using free OpenStreetMap data.

A paid maps API charges per "element", which is one origin-to-destination pair. Google's Route Matrix, for example, charges about $5 per 1,000 elements once you pass the first 10,000 free each month.

That sounds small until you count:

  • You get 1,000 orders a day.
  • For each order, you check the road distance of 20 nearby riders.
  • That's 20,000 elements a day, or about 600,000 a month.

That comes to roughly $2,000 to $2,500 a month for one feature. It doubles when your orders double. And that's before you refresh ETAs while riders are moving.

With Valhalla running on your own servers, the cost is the server, and it's fixed. A million lookups cost the same as ten million. Your vehicle positions also never leave your own cloud.

Why Postgres holds the accounts

Customers, phones, API keys, zones and alerts all live in Postgres.

This data is small, it changes rarely, and it has to be exactly right. Postgres has done that job reliably for decades.

Why nothing gets lost: one log, three readers

Every position goes into one log first. The log is the only source of truth.

Three readers each build their own copy from it:

  1. the in-memory table, which answers "where is it?" and "who's nearest?",
  2. Tile38, which watches zones and fires alerts,
  3. ClickHouse, which keeps the history.

No reader ever writes into another. Here's why that matters.

Say the history database crashes for 20 minutes. Live search doesn't care, because it reads the log, not the history database. When history comes back, it picks up where it stopped and catches up, with nothing missing.

The same goes for alerts. If the alert engine restarts, it replays what it missed. So a crossing that happened while it was down still fires.

The log keeps positions for 24 hours, which is plenty of time to fix whatever broke. Events, like "this alert fired", are kept for 7 days.

Why the system doesn't store orders

The system stores customers, phones, zones and alerts. It doesn't store orders, prices or trips, and that's on purpose.

A delivery company, an ambulance service and a wildlife group all track vehicles, but their "orders" look nothing alike:

  • A delivery has a basket and a fee.
  • An ambulance call has a patient and a priority.
  • A collared elephant has no order at all.

Build in a delivery order, and the system works well for delivery companies. But the ambulance service and the elephant reserve would have to fight it every day.

So it focuses on what every fleet needs, and answers one question really well: where are the vehicles, and what did they do? Your orders stay in your own system, which knows them better than any tracking system could.

So the first job is getting positions in, and that starts when a rider's phone logs in.

04 Logging in

A phone is checked once, then trusted.

Here's what happens when a rider starts a shift.

  1. The phone connects over MQTT with its own username and password.
  2. NATS asks the login service: "Is this phone allowed in?"
  3. The login service checks Postgres, once.
  4. If the answer is yes, it hands back a short permission slip. The slip lets the phone publish to one channel, its own, and nothing else.

From then on, every ping goes straight into the log. The database isn't touched again until the phone reconnects.

There's one more safety rule. The system takes a vehicle's identity from the channel the broker verified, never from what's written inside the message.

Say someone hacks the rider app and writes "I am vehicle 42" inside the message. It makes no difference. The broker already knows which phone logged in on that channel, and that's the identity the system trusts.

Revoking a phone is one change in Postgres, plus a kick that ends its current connection. The next time it tries to connect, the answer is no.

Once the pings are flowing, the first question anyone asks is the simplest one: where is this driver right now?

05 Where is this driver?

The answer is one row, read from memory.

This is the question from the phone-call example at the start. The agent shouldn't have to search a map. They should just see where the rider is.

Every API server keeps a live table in memory, with one row per vehicle. Each row holds:

  • where the vehicle is,
  • which way it's facing,
  • how fast it's going,
  • when the phone recorded that position.

Each new ping replaces that vehicle's row. So when your system asks "where is rider 42?", the server reads one row from memory. There's no database trip and no network trip, and the answer comes back in well under a millisecond.

The answer also says how old the position is, and whether the vehicle still counts as live.

Here's why that matters. A rider drives into a basement parking garage and loses signal. A simple system keeps showing their last dot as if it's fresh, and the dispatcher hands them an order they can't even see.

The tracking system knows the last ping was, say, 3 minutes ago. After 2 minutes of silence, it marks the vehicle as not live and leaves it out of "who's nearest?" searches. The dispatcher sees the truth: last seen 3 minutes ago, at the mall.

The same table also places each vehicle in a hexagon on the map, and that's what makes the next question fast.

06 Nearest rider

Finding the nearest rider without checking every rider.

The simple way is to measure the distance from the pickup to every vehicle, then sort the list.

With 50 vehicles, that's fine. With 10,000 vehicles and thousands of searches a minute, the system would spend all day measuring riders on the far side of the city.

So the map is split into H3 hexagon cells, each about 460 m along one edge. Think of each cell as a drawer. Every vehicle sits in the drawer for the spot it's in right now.

To find riders near a pickup, the system opens the pickup's drawer and the rings of drawers around it, and only measures the vehicles inside them. Riders 15 km away are never even looked at.

How many rings of drawers to open

rings = (radius + 2 edges) ÷ 1.5 edges, rounded up

Here's what each part does:

  • Divide by 1.5 edges. Hexagons don't line up in straight rows the way squares do. So each new ring only reaches about 1.5 edges further out in its worst direction.
  • Add 1 edge. The pickup might sit in a corner of its hexagon, not the middle, so one edge is added to cover that.
  • Add 1 more edge. That's one spare ring, just for safety.

Here's a worked example. A customer at a mall garage in the city centre wants riders within 1 km. Each edge is about 460 m.

  • Radius plus 2 edges: 1,000 m + 920 m = 1,920 m.
  • One ring reaches 1.5 edges: 1.5 × 460 m = 690 m.
  • 1,920 ÷ 690 = 2.8, which rounds up to 3 rings.

Three rings reach at least 1.5 × 3 + 0.5 = 5 edges, which is about 2.3 km. That's comfortably past the 1 km the customer asked for, even with the pickup on a corner. A test checks this against a slow search that measures every single vehicle, and the fast search has never missed one.

Skipping drawers that are clearly too far

The outer ring often includes cells whose centre is well outside the search radius, so nothing in them could ever count. Skipping those cells made searches about 5× faster.

Which way a driver is heading changes the ranking

Each vehicle's distance is multiplied by a factor based on where it's heading:

  • If it's driving away from the pickup, it counts as further away than it really is.
  • If it's driving toward the pickup, it counts as closer.

Remember the two vans heading for the depot? Heading only changes the order of the list. Nobody is ever removed from it.

The search radius is capped at 5 km. Each search returns 10 vehicles by default, and up to 100 if you ask.

All of this runs in memory, and that's exactly why Redis wouldn't help here. The whole search takes less time than a single round trip to a Redis server.

But nearest in a straight line isn't always nearest. Cities have rivers, highways and one-way streets.

07 By road

Ranking riders by the road they'll actually drive.

A rider 800 m away across the Black River is not close. To reach you, they might have to go 3 km round to the nearest bridge.

A straight-line ranking puts that rider first, and the customer waits.

So after the hexagon search builds a shortlist, the road step asks Valhalla for the real driving distance of every vehicle on it, in one call of up to 1,000 vehicles. The answer comes back in about a quarter of a second.

The shortcut that didn't work

The first plan tried to save work:

  1. Take the closest few riders by straight line.
  2. Add a few extras as a safety margin.
  3. Ask Valhalla about them in small batches.

On a test, that plan found only 7 of the true top 10 riders by road.

Roads reshuffle the list too much. A rider who looks far in a straight line can be right there by road, and the other way round. A small safety margin can't catch them all.

True top 10 by road
    The shortcut's top 10

      So now it's one big call, with two limits:

      • Any route that needs a detour of more than 3× the search radius is dropped.
      • Any vehicle more than 200 m from a road is left out.

      The response also tells your app whether the ranking is exact or partly estimated, so your app knows when it's being given a guess.

      Each vehicle has a type: motorcycle, car, pickup or van. A motorbike can take routes a van can't, and the routing knows the difference.

      What road distance still can't tell you

      There's no live traffic. Valhalla knows the roads and the speed limits, but not today's crash on the N2.

      Road distance is a much better guess than a straight line, but it's still a guess.

      Finding vehicles is half the job. The other half is knowing when one gets somewhere, without anyone watching the map.

      08 Zones and alerts

      Knowing the moment a vehicle enters or leaves an area.

      Two words matter here: a zone, and an alert.

      A zone

      A saved shape.

      A circle, or a polygon with up to 100 corners. On its own, it does nothing. It's like a line drawn on a map.

      An alert

      What makes something happen.

      It watches one vehicle for one crossing, either entering a zone or leaving it. When that crossing happens, the alert fires once, and it's done.

      Four ways people can use it

      1Sending a one-time code when the rider reaches the gate

      A customer in Sea Point orders dinner. You set an alert on a 100 m circle around their gate.

      When the rider enters that circle, the customer gets a one-time PIN (OTP) on their phone. They read it out at the door, and the rider types it into their app.

      That code proves the rider was really there and that the food reached the right person. Because the alert fires once, the customer gets one code, not three codes to choose between.

      2Waking you up when your car leaves without you

      A small tracker sits in your car, and it's paired with your phone. You set an alert: tell me if my car is more than 2 km from my phone (or 500 m, if you want it tighter).

      At 3 a.m., while you're asleep, your car starts moving down the road. Your phone stays where it is.

      As soon as the gap passes the limit, the alert calls your webhook. Your server sends you an SMS, or even rings your phone to wake you up. You find out in minutes, not in the morning when you walk out to an empty driveway.

      3Catching a truck that leaves the depot at night

      A transport company parks its trucks in a fenced yard in Montague Gardens. The last driver clocks out at 8 p.m., and nobody should move a truck again until 5 a.m.

      Each evening, the company's own system sets one exit alert per truck on the yard's polygon, set to run until 5 a.m.

      At 1:40 a.m., one truck rolls out through the gate. Its next ping is outside the polygon, so the alert fires within a second. The control room gets a webhook with the truck's plate and position, and calls the security company while the truck is still a few streets away.

      The other trucks stay quiet, because nothing crossed. In the morning, the alerts that never fired just expire.

      The fence can follow the real block, not a circle.

      A zone doesn't have to be a circle. City blocks are uneven, and a circle drawn around one spills over the streets next to it.

      With a circle, a van can leave the block and still count as inside for hundreds of metres. With the block's real shape, the exit alert fires the moment the van crosses the edge.

      4Keeping kids out of the rain while they wait for the bus

      Your child gets picked up at 6:30 a.m. But school buses are never exactly on time. Traffic, a slow child three stops earlier, or a flat tyre can shift the pickup by 15 or 20 minutes. One day the bus comes at 6:25, the next at 6:45.

      Parents don't want their child to miss the bus, so most kids get sent out early to stand at the gate. In winter, that means standing in the dark and the cold, and sometimes in the rain, for 20 minutes or more. Younger kids end up waiting alone on the pavement.

      Here's how an alert fixes that:

      1. The bus carries a tracker, or the driver's phone sends its position.
      2. Each family gets an alert on a circle of about 200 m around their gate. In a neighbourhood, that's roughly a minute away at bus speed.
      3. When the bus enters that circle, the parent's phone buzzes: "The bus is about a minute away."

      The child waits inside, warm and dry. When the phone buzzes, they put on their bag and walk out, and they reach the gate just as the bus pulls up.

      The school benefits too. It can see which buses are running late that morning, and warn parents before they start to worry.

      Why each alert fires exactly once

      Phones sometimes resend the same ping, and servers sometimes restart halfway through a job. So the same crossing can be seen twice.

      When an alert fires, Postgres flips it from "active" to "fired" in one step that only one process can win. If a second attempt comes in, it finds the alert already fired and resends the same event instead of creating a new one.

      Why alerts expire within 24 hours

      You send a rider out with an order, and you set an alert for when they reach the customer.

      On the way, the rider has an accident. They never arrive, so the alert never fires. It just sits there, waiting.

      Now picture that happening a few times a week, across all your customers, for a whole year. You end up with thousands of alerts waiting for crossings that will never happen.

      Each one is a watcher inside Tile38, and every new ping gets checked against all of them. Bit by bit, the system slows down because of alerts nobody remembers making.

      The 24-hour limit cleans them up by itself. Any alert that hasn't fired within a day expires.

      When an alert does fire, your server needs to hear about it fast, and only once.

      09 Webhooks

      Getting alerts to your server, even on a bad day.

      When an alert fires, an event goes into the event log. A separate program, the sender, delivers it to your server as a signed webhook.

      It uses the Standard Webhooks format, so you can check signatures with a free, ready-made library in most programming languages instead of writing your own. You can also change your signing secret any time, and send yourself a test event to check that everything is wired up.

      How retries work

      If your server doesn't answer, the sender waits and tries again after:

      5 s → 10 s → 30 s → 1 min → 5 min → 30 min → 2 h → 5 h → 10 h

      Each wait gets a small random nudge. Here's why.

      Your server comes back after an outage, and a thousand events are waiting. Without the nudge, they'd all retry in the same second and knock your server straight over again. The nudge spreads them out.

      After 10 tries, the sender gives up on that event. If an address hasn't worked for 24 hours, it gets switched off.

      Why every customer gets its own lane

      Picture one shared queue for everyone's events.

      Another customer's server is having a bad day. It takes 30 seconds to answer each message, and their events start blocking the queue.

      At that exact moment, your car is being stolen. Your theft alert sits in the queue, stuck behind theirs. By the time it reaches you, the car has left the street.

      With a lane per customer, that can't happen. In a test, one customer's server was set to take 30 seconds on every call. Search stayed fast, and the other customer still got their events within the same second.

      Keeping webhooks from being misused

      Webhooks only go to public internet addresses. A customer can't point one at a private address inside the tracking system's network to poke around where they shouldn't.

      Alerts tell you what's happening now. When someone asks what happened last night, you need the trail.

      10 Replay

      Replay any trip, and the argument ends.

      Most disputes in this business come down to one question: where was the vehicle? Replay answers it with facts.

      Here's a common case. A customer calls in, upset. They say they waited at the gate for 10 minutes and nobody came. They never got a call, and never got a notification that the rider had arrived. Maybe the pizza went back to the shop. Maybe the rider ate it.

      Today, that's an argument. The rider says one thing and the customer says another, and support has to pick who to believe.

      With replay, you open the rider's trail for that evening. If the rider stood outside that gate for 10 minutes, you'll see it, minute by minute. If they never got there, you'll see that too. The argument ends in a minute, with proof either way, and you can refund or push back fairly.

      Three ways to view a trip

      Raw

      Exactly what the phone sent, jumps and wobbles included. Use it when you need the unedited record.

      Smooth

      Cleans the GPS noise into a steady line, which is easier to read at a glance.

      Road

      Snaps the trail onto real streets, with a score that says how confident the match is. Use it to see which roads the vehicle actually took.

      How positions get into history

      A separate worker reads the log and writes positions into ClickHouse in batches: every 10,000 rows or every second, whichever comes first. Writing one row at a time would be far slower.

      Late pings are kept too. Say a rider's phone loses signal in a tunnel, then sends a backlog of positions on the other side. Those positions still land in the right place on the trail.

      History is erased one customer at a time, with a single command. The command waits until the data is really gone from disk.

      Delivery is where this started, but nothing in it is really about food.

      11 Who it's for

      Anything that moves can use it.

      This isn't only for food delivery. Any team that needs to know where moving things are, and what they did, can build on it. Here's how different teams could use it, starting with the problem each one has today. Pick a team to see what changes, or pick a tool to see who uses it.

      Whichever team you're on, the next question is the same: what does it cost to run?

      A small fleet mostly pays for the minimum of three servers, which is what keeps your data safe when one dies. A large fleet pays a few cents per vehicle a month.

      There's also no maps bill. Compare that with the roughly $2,000 a month a paid matrix API could cost a mid-sized delivery business for road distances alone.

      That's what is built and running today. Here's what comes next.

      13 What's coming next

      Seven things are on the way.

      None of these are built yet. Each one comes from a real problem the current system leaves open.

      1. An email when your server is down.

        Today, a failing webhook address keeps getting retried, then gets switched off after 24 hours. You might not notice until customers complain. Next, you'll get an email as soon as failures start, while the retries are still holding your events.

      2. A webhook for alerts that never fired.

        Remember the rider who crashed and never arrived? Today, that alert expires quietly. Next, you'll get a webhook when it does. A delivery alert that never fired is often a sign something went wrong on the road, and someone should check on the rider.

      3. Alerts with no time limit.

        Some zones need watching forever, like the fence around a reserve. The alert should fire every time the elephant leaves, and every time it comes back, all year round. These alerts will fire on every crossing, with their own safeguards so they can't pile up.

      4. A webhook when a vehicle runs late.

        Give the system a planned route and an expected arrival time. If the vehicle falls behind, you'll hear about it while there's still time to act: warn the customer, send a second rider, or call the driver.

      5. A webhook when a vehicle goes off course.

        Running late and going off course are different problems. A van can be right on time and still be somewhere it shouldn't be.

        Here's how it will work. You give the system the planned route, and it draws a corridor around it, say 300 m on each side. If the vehicle leaves that corridor and stays out for more than a couple of minutes, your server gets a webhook. The short wait stops a quick detour round a roadblock from setting it off.

        This catches a lot: a cash van forced off its route, a rider doing a side job in the middle of your delivery, a driver who took a wrong turn and is heading the wrong way before the customer starts calling, and a truck carrying high-value goods that stops somewhere it was never meant to be.

      6. An alert when two moving things come close to each other.

        Today, every alert watches one vehicle against a fixed zone on the map. But some of the most useful moments happen when two things that are both moving get close: a vehicle and a person, or two vehicles.

        It fits ride-hailing pickups (the passenger's phone buzzes when the driver is 100 m away), rider handovers (logged the moment two riders are within 50 m), cash-in-transit escorts (an unknown tracked vehicle stays close to a cash van for too long), and tow trucks (the stranded driver hears when help is 2 minutes away). It also completes the car-tracker example: that alert fires when your car and your phone drift apart, and this one fires when two things come together.

      7. One year of history instead of 90 days.

        The 90 days was for testing and the demo. Many businesses need a full year for audits, insurance claims and seasonal trends. Each position takes so little space that keeping a year is affordable.

      The short version

      Tracking is plumbing. Build it once.

      Proven tools, fitted together, run on three small servers. Your team spends its time on what customers see.
